newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore managers most stressed, study says.
newsitem.headline: Singapore managers most stressed, study says.

text.p: Business managers in Singapore are among the most stressed by information overload, an international study released Monday showed.
The survey of 1,313 executives in Singapore, the United States, Hong Kong, Britain and Australia found substantial numbers suffering from an information glut.

"The worldwide burden of keeping up with the information explosion has led to soaring executive stress, loss of job satisfaction and phsyical ill-health," psychologist David Lewis, who analysed the survey results, said in the foreword.
The report, "Dying for Information?", was commissioned from Britain's Benchmark Research by Reuters Business Information, part of international news and information organisation Reuters Holdings Plc.

Asked on a scale of one to five whether they agreed with the statement, "I often suffer stress as a result of the quantity of material on a day-to-day basis," Singaporean managers averaged 3.0, compared with 2.8 for the United States, 2.7 for Hong Kong, 2.6 for Britain, and 2.5 for Australia.

Sixty-eight percent of Singapore's managers said they expect the next two years to be more, or far more stressful than today. This compared with 58 percent in Britain, 54 percent in the U.S., 51 percent in Australia and 46 percent in Hong Kong.

"Having too much information can be as dangerous as having too little," Lewis said. "It can lead to a paralysis of analysis, making it far harder to find the right solutions or make the best decisions."
Of all managers questioned, 49 percent said they are frequently unable to handle the volumes of information they receive, while two thirds said information is under-utilised.
And 48 percent believe the Internet will add further to the information burden in the next two years.
"What this report makes crystal clear is that finding ways of dealing with the information burden is now one of the most urgent world-wide challenges facing business," Lewis said.
